title: Adherence to risk-tailored antiemetic prophylaxis and rescue treatment for nausea and vomiting after day surgery
subtitle: Case-control study of under- and over-prophylaxis
statement: In a day surgery unit of about 6,000 adult procedures a year, about one patient in eight needs a rescue antiemetic in recovery and nausea is the commonest reason for unplanned overnight stays, two years after a risk-tailored prophylaxis protocol was adopted. It is not known how often prophylaxis matches the protocol, or whether patients who receive less than recommended are more likely to need rescue treatment. Because the drug section of the anaesthetic record is on paper, a design that reads a limited number of records is needed. No time or data limits were stated with the request.
whoAffected: Adults having day surgery, especially those with high risk scores, their carers who expect them home the same day, recovery nurses and anaesthetists.
whatHurts: Nausea and vomiting are distressing, delay discharge and cause unplanned overnight stays; extra antiemetics can sedate patients and delay discharge too.
currentPractice: Four-factor risk score and one to three antiemetic agents by score; drugs recorded on the paper section of the anaesthetic record; rescue treatment recorded in the recovery nausea log.
whyNow: The protocol has been in place for two years without any check of adherence, and unplanned stays are rising.
patientCenteredGoal: Every patient receives the prophylaxis their risk calls for and goes home on the day of surgery without nausea or sedation holding them back.
summary: Problem framed as a question about prophylaxis adherence and rescue treatment; the need states no constraints.
